title: Ἡ σχεδίη
about: Calypso leads Odysseus back to her cave, where they eat, she of ambrosia and he of mortal food, and she asks him one last time whether he truly wants to go home, telling him that if he knew what sorrows lay ahead he would stay with her and be immortal, and that she is surely no less lovely than his wife. Odysseus grants that Penelope cannot match a goddess, yet says he longs every day for home, and will bear whatever a god sends him at sea. They spend the night together. At dawn Calypso gives him an axe and an adze, shows him where the tallest dry trees grow, and brings augers and cloth for sails; in four days he fells and shapes the timber and builds a broad craft with deck, mast, yard, steering-oar and a wicker bulwark, and drags it down to the sea. On the fifth day she bathes and dresses him, stocks the craft with wine, water and food, and sends a gentle wind. He sails for seventeen days, steering by the stars as she told him and never sleeping, and on the eighteenth the mountains of the Phaeacians' land come into view. But Poseidon, returning from the Ethiopians, sees him from far off, and in anger resolves that he will yet give Odysseus his fill of trouble.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’ ἡγήσατο δῖα θεάων
καρπαλίμως·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, the heavenly-one of goddesses led the way,
swiftly;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and she who is heavenly even among goddesses led the way swiftly;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’ is the feminine closing formula of the house table, ‘So then having spoken’: Calypso has just finished speaking. ἡγήσατο is the aorist of ἡγέομαι ‘lead the way’. δῖα θεάων ‘heavenly-one of goddesses’ stands here without the name, and by itself means Calypso; θεάων is a first-declension genitive plural in -άων, Attic θεῶν. καρπαλίμως ‘swiftly’ runs over into the next line, and an ano teleia closes the clause.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα μετ’ ἴχνια βαῖνε θεοῖο.
sentences.l: And he then walked following in the footsteps of the god.
sentences.i: and he followed close behind in the footsteps of the god.
sentences.n: This half-line is word for word the one used at 2.406 and 3.30, where Telemachus walked behind Athena, and it keeps that unit’s English. ὁ is ‘he’, the pronoun. βαῖνε is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘went on walking’. μετ’ ἴχνια is ‘after the tracks’. θεοῖο is a genitive in -οιο; θεός serves in Homer for a goddess as well as a god, so ‘the god’ here is Calypso.

sentences.t:
ἷξον δὲ σπεῖος γλαφυρὸν θεὸς ἠδὲ καὶ ἀνήρ,
καί ῥ’ ὁ μὲν ἔνθα καθέζετ’ ἐπὶ θρόνου ἔνθεν ἀνέστη
Ἑρμείας, νύμφη δ’ ἐτίθει πάρα πᾶσαν ἐδωδήν,
ἔσθειν καὶ πίνειν, οἷα βροτοὶ ἄνδρες ἔδουσιν·
sentences.l:
And they reached the hollow cave, the god and the man too,
and he sat down there upon the chair from which had risen
Hermes, and the nymph set beside him every kind of food,
to eat and to drink, such as mortal men eat;
sentences.i: They reached the hollow cave, the goddess and the man together, and he sat down on the chair from which Hermes had risen, and the nymph set food of every kind before him, to eat and to drink, such as mortal men eat;
sentences.n: ἷξον is an unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’. σπεῖος is the epic form of σπέος ‘cave’, and γλαφυρόν keeps the house ‘hollow’. θεός is again feminine in sense: ‘god and man’ is the pair. ῥ’ is ἄρα. καθέζετ’ is καθέζετο, and ἔνθα … ἔνθεν is ‘there … from where’. Ἑρμείας, the epic form of Hermes’ name, runs over into 196. πάρα, with the accent thrown back, is the adverb ‘beside’. ἔσθειν is an epic by-form of ἐσθίειν, and ἔδουσιν comes from ἔδω ‘eat’: mortal food, set against the next line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ δ’ ἀντίον ἷζεν Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο,
τῇ δὲ παρ’ ἀμβροσίην δμῳαὶ καὶ νέκταρ ἔθηκαν.
sentences.l:
And she herself sat facing divine Odysseus,
and beside her ambrosia the serving-women and nectar set.
sentences.i: She herself sat down facing divine Odysseus, and the serving-women set ambrosia and nectar beside her.
sentences.n: αὐτή is ‘she herself’. ἀντίον with the genitive is ‘opposite, facing’. ἷζεν is the unaugmented imperfect of ἵζω ‘sit’. Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο has θεῖος ‘divine’, as the table fixes it. τῇ is ‘for her’, and παρ’ … ἔθηκαν ‘set beside’ is tmesis. δμῳαί are ‘serving-women’, bondwomen of the house. Ambrosia and nectar are the food and drink of the gods: the two sit at one table, and each eats what belongs to their kind.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: A whole line of the feast-formulas, already met at 1.149 and kept in its English. ὀνείαθ’ is ὀνείατα ‘good things’, food, with the τ roughened to θ before the rough breathing of ἑτοῖμα. προκείμενα is the participle of πρόκειμαι ‘lie set before’. ἴαλλον is the unaugmented imperfect of ἰάλλω ‘send forth, put out (the hand)’. οἱ is ‘they’, here the pair.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τάρπησαν ἐδητύος ἠδὲ ποτῆτος,
τοῖς ἄρα μύθων ἦρχε Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων·
sentences.l:
But when they had had their fill of food and of drink,
among them then of speeches made-beginning Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses:
sentences.i: But when they had had their fill of food and drink, Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τάρπησαν is an aorist passive of τέρπω, ‘have one’s fill of’, with the genitive. ἐδητύος and ποτῆτος are epic nouns, ‘food’ and ‘drink’. The second line is the table’s speech-introduction τοῖς ἄρα μύθων ἦρχε, filled here with Calypso’s name and epithet: ἄρχω with the genitive μύθων is ‘begin the speeches’. ‘Among them’ here means the pair. The ano teleia does the work of a colon before the speech.

sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
is it so, then, that home to your dear fatherland
at once, now, you wish to go?
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, so you really wish to go home, at once, now, to your dear fatherland?
sentences.n: The first line is a whole-line address: διογενές is the vocative of διογενής ‘Zeus-born’, Λαερτιάδη the vocative of the patronymic ‘son of Laertes’, πολυμήχαν’ the elided vocative of πολυμήχανος ‘many-devising’, and Ὀδυσσεῦ the vocative of the name. οὕτω δή is ‘just so, then’. οἶκόνδε, with the suffix -δε ‘to’, and ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν say the direction twice. ἰέναι is the infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’. αὐτίκα νῦν presses the haste: ‘right away, now’.

sentences.t: σὺ δὲ χαῖρε καὶ ἔμπης.
sentences.l: But you, farewell, all the same.
sentences.i: Still, fare you well, all the same.
sentences.n: χαῖρε is the ordinary greeting, and serves at a meeting and at a parting alike; here, after the question, it is a farewell. σὺ δέ is ‘but you’. ἔμπης is ‘all the same, nevertheless’: she lets him go while making plain that she disapproves. The table’s χαῖρε, ξεῖνε ‘Welcome, stranger’ is the other use of the same imperative.

sentences.t:
εἴ γε μὲν εἰδείης σῇσι φρεσὶν ὅσσα τοι αἶσα
κήδε’ ἀναπλῆσαι, πρὶν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι,
sentences.l:
Yet if you knew in your own mind how many, for you, it is your lot
of sorrows to fill up, before reaching your fatherland,
sentences.i: But if you knew in your mind how many sorrows it is your lot to fill up before you reach your fatherland,
sentences.n: The sentence runs from 206 to 210, five lines, so it is cut here at the comma between the condition and its conclusion. εἰ with the optative εἰδείης (perfect optative of οἶδα) is a remote condition. σῇσι φρεσίν is a dative plural in -ῃσι, ‘in your mind’. ὅσσα is ὅσα with epic σσ. τοι is σοι, and αἶσα ‘portion, lot’ takes an understood ἐστί. κήδε’ is uncontracted κήδεα (Attic κήδη) ‘sorrows, troubles’. ἀναπλῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀναπίμπλημι ‘fill up’, as one fills a measure. πρίν takes the infinitive.

sentences.t:
ἐνθάδε κ’ αὖθι μένων σὺν ἐμοὶ τόδε δῶμα φυλάσσοις
ἀθάνατός τ’ εἴης, ἱμειρόμενός περ ἰδέσθαι
σὴν ἄλοχον, τῆς τ’ αἰὲν ἐέλδεαι ἤματα πάντα.
sentences.l:
here, staying on in this very place with me, you would keep this house
and be immortal, longing though you are to see
your wife, for whom you yearn always, all your days.
sentences.i: you would stay on here with me and keep this house, and be immortal, however much you long to see your wife, whom you yearn for always, all your days.
sentences.n: κ’ is κε, the epic ἄν, with the optatives φυλάσσοις and εἴης: ‘you would keep … and be’. ἐνθάδε … αὖθι is ‘here, in this very place’. φυλάσσω ‘guard, keep’ is here ‘stay in and keep’ the house. ἱμειρόμενός περ has concessive περ, where Attic would write καίπερ. σὴν ἄλοχον is ‘your wife’. τῆς is a genitive with ἐέλδεαι ‘you long for’, an uncontracted second singular (Attic -ῃ). ἤματα πάντα keeps the table’s ‘all your days’.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν θην κείνης γε χερείων εὔχομαι εἶναι,
οὐ δέμας οὐδὲ φυήν, ἐπεὶ οὔ πως οὐδὲ ἔοικεν
θνητὰς ἀθανάτῃσι δέμας καὶ εἶδος ἐρίζειν.
sentences.l:
Surely I do not claim to be worse than that woman,
not in body nor in stature, since it is in no way fitting
for mortal women with immortal ones in body and looks to vie.”
sentences.i: Surely I can claim to be no worse than she is, in body or in stature, since it is not at all fitting for mortal women to vie with immortals in body and in looks.”
sentences.n: θην is an affirming particle, ‘surely, I think’, with a touch of irony. κείνης is ἐκείνης, a genitive of comparison with χερείων, an epic comparative of κακός (Attic χείρων). εὔχομαι here is ‘I claim, declare’, not ‘I pray’. δέμας, φυήν and εἶδος are accusatives of respect, ‘in body, in stature, in looks’. ἔοικεν is ‘it is fitting’. θνητάς is feminine, ‘mortal women’, and ἀθανάτῃσι has the dative plural -ῃσι. Calypso never names Penelope: κείνης ‘that woman’ is all she allows her.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: The table’s reply-formula τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη, filled with Odysseus’ name and πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’. Calypso has just called him πολυμήχανος ‘many-devising’ at 203; the two epithets are different words and are kept apart in English. ἀπαμειβόμενος is the present middle participle ‘answering’, and προσέφη is ‘addressed’. τήν is ‘her’, the pronoun.

sentences.t: πότνα θεά, μή μοι τόδε χώεο·
sentences.l: “Lady goddess, do not for this be angry with me;
sentences.i: “Lady goddess, do not be angry with me for this;
sentences.n: πότνα is a short vocative form of πότνια ‘lady, mistress’, the title already given Calypso in the ‘lady nymph’ of 1.14. μή with the present imperative χώεο (uncontracted, Attic χώου) forbids what may be under way: ‘do not be angry’. μοι is a dative of the person one is angry with. τόδε is an accusative of respect, ‘for this’. His first words are placating.

sentences.t:
οἶδα καὶ αὐτὸς
πάντα μάλ’, οὕνεκα σεῖο περίφρων Πηνελόπεια
εἶδος ἀκιδνοτέρη μέγεθός τ’ εἰσάντα ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.i: I know it very well myself, that circumspect Penelope is slighter than you in looks and in stature, to look upon face to face;
sentences.n: οἶδα καὶ αὐτός is ‘I know it myself too’, and πάντα μάλ’ is ‘full well’. οὕνεκα here means ‘that’, where it usually means ‘because’. σεῖο is σοῦ, a genitive of comparison. περίφρων Πηνελόπεια keeps the table’s ‘circumspect’. ἀκιδνοτέρη is the comparative of ἀκιδνός ‘slight, feeble, of little account’, a rare word. εἶδος μέγεθός τ’ are accusatives of respect, and he takes over Calypso’s own εἶδος from 213. εἰσάντα ἰδέσθαι is ‘to look at face to face’.

sentences.t: ἡ μὲν γὰρ βροτός ἐστι, σὺ δ’ ἀθάνατος καὶ ἀγήρως.
sentences.l: for she is mortal, but you immortal and ageless.
sentences.i: for she is mortal, and you are immortal and ageless.
sentences.n: ἡ is ‘she’, the pronoun. βροτός and ἀθάνατος are adjectives of two terminations, so the masculine-looking forms serve for women. ἀγήρως is the contracted form of ἀγήραος ‘ageless’ (ἀ- + γῆρας ‘old age’). μέν … δέ sets the two women side by side. He grants the whole of Calypso’s point before he refuses her.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὣς ἐθέλω καὶ ἐέλδομαι ἤματα πάντα
οἴκαδέ τ’ ἐλθέμεναι καὶ νόστιμον ἦμαρ ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.l:
But even so I wish and I yearn all my days
to come home and see the homecoming day.
sentences.i: But even so I wish and I yearn, all my days, to come home and see the day of my homecoming.
sentences.n: καὶ ὥς is ‘even so’: accented ὥς is the adverb, Attic οὕτως. ἐέλδομαι takes up Calypso’s ἐέλδεαι of 210: she said he yearned for his wife, and he answers that he yearns for home. ἤματα πάντα is ‘all my days’, as in her line. Line 220 is word for word a line of 3.233 and keeps its English there. ἐλθέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι (Attic ἐλθεῖν). νόστιμον ἦμαρ keeps the table’s ‘the homecoming day’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ αὖ τις ῥαίῃσι θεῶν ἐνὶ οἴνοπι πόντῳ,
τλήσομαι ἐν στήθεσσιν ἔχων ταλαπενθέα θυμόν·
sentences.l:
And if again some one of the gods shatters me on the wine-faced open-sea,
I shall endure, having in my breast a grief-enduring heart;
sentences.i: And if some god shatters me again on the sea that has the look of wine, I shall endure it, with a heart in my breast that can bear grief;
sentences.n: εἰ with the subjunctive ῥαίῃσι, and no κε, is epic. ῥαίῃσι is a present subjunctive with the epic ending -ῃσι, from ῥαίω ‘shatter, wreck’; its object, himself and his craft, is understood. αὖ ‘again’ admits it has happened before. ἐνί is ἐν, and οἴνοπι πόντῳ keeps the table’s ‘wine-faced open-sea’. τλήσομαι is the future of τλάω ‘endure’, the root of ταλαπενθέα ‘grief-enduring’ and of his epithet πολύτλας. στήθεσσιν has the dative plural -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ μάλα πολλὰ πάθον καὶ πολλὰ μόγησα
κύμασι καὶ πολέμῳ·
sentences.l:
For already very many things I have suffered, and many I have toiled through,
in waves and in war;
sentences.i: For I have suffered a great deal already, and toiled through much, on the waves and in war;
sentences.n: πάθον is an unaugmented aorist of πάσχω (Attic ἔπαθον), and μόγησα an unaugmented aorist of μογέω ‘toil, labour’. πολλὰ … πολλά repeats the word, as the poem’s opening did with πολλά and πολλῶν. κύμασι καὶ πολέμῳ are datives of circumstance, ‘amid waves and war’: two words for his years at sea and his years at Troy. ἤδη is ‘already’.

sentences.t: μετὰ καὶ τόδε τοῖσι γενέσθω.
sentences.l: among them let this too come to pass.”
sentences.i: let this be added to the rest.”
sentences.n: μετά is an adverb here, ‘among, in addition’, with τοῖσι ‘to those’, the sufferings of the line before. γενέσθω is the third singular aorist imperative of γίγνομαι, ‘let it be’. The speech closes, and in the Greek it is five words: whatever this new trouble is, it will join the others. Odysseus’ reply is as long as Calypso’s speech, and he never answers her offer of immortality directly.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ἠέλιος δ’ ἄρ’ ἔδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθεν·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the sun then set, and darkness came on;
sentences.i: So he spoke; and the sun set, and darkness came on;
sentences.n: The table’s evening formula after ὣς ἔφατ’, ‘So he spoke’. The line matches 3.329 except for its final ν and its punctuation, and keeps that line’s English with a semicolon for the ano teleia. ἠέλιος is the epic form of ἥλιος. ἔδυ is the root aorist of δύω ‘sink, set’. ἐπὶ … ἦλθεν is tmesis, ‘came on’. κνέφας is ‘darkness, dusk’.

sentences.t:
ἐλθόντες δ’ ἄρα τώ γε μυχῷ σπείους γλαφυροῖο
τερπέσθην φιλότητι, παρ’ ἀλλήλοισι μένοντες.
sentences.l:
and going, then, the two of them, into the inmost part of the hollow cave,
took their joy in love, remaining beside one another.
sentences.i: and the two of them went into the innermost part of the hollow cave and took their joy in love, staying beside each other.
sentences.n: τώ γε is a dual pronoun, ‘the two of them’, and τερπέσθην is a dual, unaugmented past form of τέρπομαι ‘take delight’; the participles ἐλθόντες and μένοντες are plural, and Homer mixes dual and plural freely. μυχῷ is a dative of place, ‘in the inmost recess’. σπείους is the genitive of σπέος with epic ει. φιλότητι is the plain word for love-making, as in μίγη φιλότητι at 5.126. It is their last night.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
αὐτίχ’ ὁ μὲν χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε ἕννυτ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
sentences.l:
When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn,
at once he, Odysseus, put on both cloak and tunic,
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, Odysseus at once put on his cloak and tunic,
sentences.n: The first line is the table’s whole-line dawn formula and keeps its fixed English. The sentence runs 228–232, five lines, so it is cut here at the comma where ὁ μέν ‘he’ gives way to αὐτὴ δ’ ‘and she herself’. αὐτίχ’ is αὐτίκα elided before a rough breathing. ἕννυτ’ is ἕννυτο, the unaugmented imperfect of ἕννυμι ‘put on (clothes)’. χλαῖνα is a thick woollen cloak, χιτών the tunic worn under it.

sentences.t:
αὐτὴ δ’ ἀργύφεον φᾶρος μέγα ἕννυτο νύμφη,
λεπτὸν καὶ χαρίεν, περὶ δὲ ζώνην βάλετ’ ἰξυῖ
καλὴν χρυσείην, κεφαλῇ δ’ ἐφύπερθε καλύπτρην.
sentences.l:
and she herself, the nymph, put on a great silver-white robe,
fine and graceful, and around her waist she threw a girdle,
fair, golden, and on her head, above, a veil.
sentences.i: and the nymph herself put on a great silver-white robe, fine and graceful, threw a fair golden girdle about her waist, and set a veil upon her head.
sentences.n: ἀργύφεον is ‘silver-white, shining white’. φᾶρος is a large woven cloth, worn by a man as a cloak and by a woman as a robe. λεπτόν is ‘fine, finely woven’. περὶ … βάλετ’ is tmesis, ‘threw around’, and ἰξυῖ is the dative of ἰξύς ‘waist’. ζώνη is ‘girdle’. The last clause borrows its verb from the one before. καλύπτρη ‘veil’ is from καλύπτω ‘cover’, the verb Calypso’s own name is usually connected with.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ Ὀδυσσῆι μεγαλήτορι μήδετο πομπήν·
sentences.l: And then for great-spirited Odysseus she devised a sending-home;
sentences.i: And then she set about planning the voyage home for great-spirited Odysseus;
sentences.n: Ὀδυσσῆι μεγαλήτορι keeps the table’s ‘great-spirited’; the dative is ‘for Odysseus’. μήδετο is the unaugmented imperfect of μήδομαι ‘devise, plan’. πομπή is ‘escort, sending on one’s way’, the conveyance a host owes a departing guest. Here there is no ship and no crew, and what follows shows what the sending amounts to: tools, timber and a wind. The ano teleia introduces the list.

sentences.t:
δῶκέν οἱ πέλεκυν μέγαν, ἄρμενον ἐν παλάμῃσι,
χάλκεον, ἀμφοτέρωθεν ἀκαχμένον·
sentences.l:
she gave him an axe, a great one, fitted to his palms,
of bronze, sharpened on both sides;
sentences.i: she gave him a great axe of bronze that fitted his grip, sharpened on both edges;
sentences.n: δῶκεν is an unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι (Attic ἔδωκεν), and οἱ is ‘to him’. πέλεκυς is ‘axe’. ἀμφοτέρωθεν ἀκαχμένον ‘sharpened on both sides’ makes it double-edged; whether that means a two-headed axe or a single blade ground on both faces the Greek does not say. ἀκαχμένον is a perfect participle ‘sharpened’, of obscure formation. ἄρμενον ‘fitted’, from ἀραρίσκω ‘fit, join’, begins a family of joining-words that runs through the building scene.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐν αὐτῷ
στειλειὸν περικαλλὲς ἐλάινον, εὖ ἐναρηρός·
sentences.l:
and in it
a haft, very beautiful, of olive-wood, well fitted in;
sentences.i: and in it was a very beautiful handle of olive-wood, firmly fitted;
sentences.n: There is no verb: ἦν is understood. αὐτῷ is the axe. στειλειόν is the ‘haft, handle’ of an axe. περικαλλές is ‘very beautiful’, with περι- intensive. ἐλάινον is ‘of olive-wood’ (ἐλαία ‘olive’). ἐναρηρός is the intransitive perfect participle of ἐναραρίσκω, ‘fitted in, fixed fast’: the same joining-verb as ἄρμενον in 234.

sentences.t: δῶκε δ’ ἔπειτα σκέπαρνον ἐύξοον·
sentences.l: and she gave him next a well-polished adze;
sentences.i: and next she gave him a well-polished adze;
sentences.n: σκέπαρνον is a woodworker’s tool for dressing timber. It is usually taken as an adze, with the blade set across the handle for shaping and smoothing, though ancient explanations also call it a kind of axe, and its exact shape is not certain. ἐύξοον keeps the table’s ‘well-polished’, from ξέω ‘smooth, plane’; the same verb returns as ξέσσε in 245, where the adze is put to work. δῶκε is unaugmented, as in 234.

sentences.t:
ἦρχε δ’ ὁδοῖο
νήσου ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῆς, ὅθι δένδρεα μακρὰ πεφύκει,
κλήθρη τ’ αἴγειρός τ’, ἐλάτη τ’ ἦν οὐρανομήκης,
αὖα πάλαι, περίκηλα, τά οἱ πλώοιεν ἐλαφρῶς.
sentences.l:
and she led the way
to the island’s far edge, where tall trees had grown,
alder and black poplar, and fir there was, heaven-high,
long since dry, dried right through, which would float lightly for him.
sentences.i: and she led the way to the far edge of the island, where tall trees had grown, alder and black poplar and fir that reached to heaven, long since dead and dry, dried right through, the kind that would float lightly for him.
sentences.n: ἦρχε ὁδοῖο is ‘led the way’, ἄρχω with the genitive. ἐσχατιῆς is ‘edge, border’. ὅθι is ‘where’, and πεφύκει the pluperfect of φύω, ‘had grown’. κλήθρη, αἴγειρος and ἐλάτη are the lexicons’ alder, black poplar and fir; ancient tree-names do not always match modern species exactly. οὐρανομήκης is ‘as tall as heaven’. αὖα is ‘dry’. περίκηλα is rare and its sense is inferred: περι- intensive and a root of burning, so ‘very dry’. πλώοιεν is an optative of πλώω, the epic form of πλέω ‘float, sail’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ δεῖξ’, ὅθι δένδρεα μακρὰ πεφύκει,
ἡ μὲν ἔβη πρὸς δῶμα Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων,
αὐτὰρ ὁ τάμνετο δοῦρα·
sentences.i: But when she had shown him where the tall trees had grown, Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, went back to the house, and he set to cutting timbers;
sentences.n: δεῖξ’ is δεῖξε, the unaugmented aorist of δείκνυμι ‘show’. ὅθι δένδρεα μακρὰ πεφύκει repeats the end of 238 word for word and keeps its English. ἔβη is ‘went’. Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων is the line-end name and epithet heard at 202, fixed in the table. τάμνετο is the imperfect middle of τάμνω, epic for τέμνω, ‘was cutting for himself’. δοῦρα is the plural of δόρυ, here in its first sense ‘tree-trunk, beam’.

sentences.t: θοῶς δέ οἱ ἤνυτο ἔργον.
sentences.l: and quickly for him was the work accomplished.
sentences.i: and the work went quickly for him.
sentences.n: θοῶς is the adverb of θοός ‘swift’, the adjective of the table’s νηῦς θοή. ἤνυτο is the imperfect passive of ἀνύω ‘accomplish’: the work ‘was getting done’. οἱ is a dative of interest, ‘for him’. ἔργον is ‘work, task’. The half-line looks forward over the four days of labour summed up at 262.

sentences.t:
εἴκοσι δ’ ἔκβαλε πάντα, πελέκκησεν δ’ ἄρα χαλκῷ,
ξέσσε δ’ ἐπισταμένως καὶ ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνεν.
sentences.l:
Twenty in all he felled, and axe-hewed them then with the bronze,
and planed them skilfully, and straightened them to the line.
sentences.i: He felled twenty in all, hewed them into shape with the bronze, planed them skilfully and trued them straight to the line.
sentences.n: ἔκβαλε is unaugmented, ‘threw down, felled’. πελέκκησεν is the aorist of πελεκκάω ‘hew with an axe’, built on πέλεκυς; χαλκῷ ‘with the bronze’ names the tool by its metal. ξέσσε is the aorist of ξέω ‘smooth, plane’, with epic σσ. ἐπισταμένως is ‘with skill’. στάθμη is the carpenter’s line, a stretched cord used to mark a straight edge, and ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνεν is ‘made straight to the line’. ἴθυνεν is unaugmented.

sentences.t: τόφρα δ’ ἔνεικε τέρετρα Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων·
sentences.l: Meanwhile she brought augers, Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses;
sentences.i: Meanwhile Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, brought him augers;
sentences.n: τόφρα is ‘meanwhile’. ἔνεικε is an aorist of φέρω ‘bring’, the epic form beside Attic ἤνεγκε, unaugmented. τέρετρα, the plural of τέρετρον, are ‘borers, augers’, tools for boring holes, from the root of τετραίνω ‘bore’ in the next line; whether hand-turned or bow-driven the text does not say. The line ends with Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων as at 202 and 242.

sentences.t:
τέτρηνεν δ’ ἄρα πάντα καὶ ἥρμοσεν ἀλλήλοισιν,
γόμφοισιν δ’ ἄρα τήν γε καὶ ἁρμονίῃσιν ἄρασσεν.
sentences.l:
and he bored them all then and fitted them to one another,
and with pegs then it, and with joinings, he hammered together.
sentences.i: He bored them all and fitted them to one another, and hammered the raft together with pegs and joinings.
sentences.n: τέτρηνεν is a reduplicated aorist of τετραίνω ‘bore through’. ἥρμοσεν is the aorist of ἁρμόζω ‘fit together’, and ἀλλήλοισιν is ‘to one another’. γόμφοι are ‘pegs, bolts’, wooden dowels driven through the bored holes. ἁρμονίαι are ‘joinings, fastenings’; the exact device is uncertain: mortise-and-tenon joints, clamps and lashings have all been proposed. τήν γε is feminine: the σχεδίη ‘raft’, not named until 251. ἄρασσεν is ‘hammered, drove home’.

sentences.t:
ὅσσον τίς τ’ ἔδαφος νηὸς τορνώσεται ἀνὴρ
φορτίδος εὐρείης, ἐὺ εἰδὼς τεκτοσυνάων,
τόσσον ἔπ’ εὐρεῖαν σχεδίην ποιήσατ’ Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l:
As wide as the floor of a ship a man lays out with rounded lines,
of a broad freighter, a man well versed in carpentry,
so wide the broad raft made Odysseus.
sentences.i: As wide as a man well versed in carpentry lays out the floor of a broad freighter with rounded lines, so wide did Odysseus make his broad raft.
sentences.n: A simile built on ὅσσον … τόσσον ‘as wide … so wide’, with epic σσ. τ’ is the epic τε of general truth. ἔδαφος is the ‘floor, bottom’ of a hull. φορτίς is a ‘freighter’, a cargo-ship (φόρτος ‘cargo’), and is broad for its cargo. τορνώσεται is an aorist subjunctive with short vowel (Attic τορνώσηται), from τορνόω ‘round off, mark out with a τόρνος’, a compass-like tool. τεκτοσυνάων is ‘carpentry’. ἔπ’, with the accent thrown back, is adverbial, and its exact force is debated. σχεδίη keeps the table’s ‘raft’, though the deck, mast and steering-oar described below are more than a raft usually has.

sentences.t:
ἴκρια δὲ στήσας, ἀραρὼν θαμέσι σταμίνεσσι,
ποίει·
sentences.l:
And setting up the decking, fitting it to close-set ribs,
he worked at it;
sentences.i: He set up the decking, fitting it to close-set ribs, and worked on it;
sentences.n: ἴκρια are ‘deck-planks, decking’. στήσας is the aorist participle of ἵστημι ‘set up’. ἀραρών is the transitive aorist participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fitting’, the joining-verb again. θαμέσι is the dative plural of θαμέες ‘close-set’. σταμίνεσσι, with the dative -εσσι, is from σταμῖνες, built on στα- ‘stand’; whether these are the ribs of the hull or upright posts carrying the deck is uncertain. ποίει is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘went on making’, running over into 253.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ μακρῇσιν ἐπηγκενίδεσσι τελεύτα.
sentences.l: but with long side-planks he finished it.
sentences.i: and he finished it off with long side-planks.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ is αὐτάρ ‘but, and then’. ἐπηγκενίδεσσι, with the dative -εσσι, is a rare word. It is usually taken to mean long planks laid along the sides over the ribs, a kind of gunwale or side-planking, but its exact referent is uncertain; ‘side-planks’ gives the usual reading and no more. μακρῇσιν has the dative -ῃσι. τελεύτα is the unaugmented, contracted imperfect of τελευτάω ‘bring to an end, finish’.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ἱστὸν ποίει καὶ ἐπίκριον ἄρμενον αὐτῷ·
sentences.l: And in it he made a mast, and a yard fitted to it;
sentences.i: He made a mast for it, and a yard fitted to the mast;
sentences.n: ἐν is an adverb, ‘in it’, meaning the craft. ἱστός is the ‘mast’; the same word means a loom, from ἵστημι, since both stand upright. ἐπίκριον is the ‘yard’, the spar fixed across the mast from which the sail hangs, a rare word. ἄρμενον ‘fitted’ is the participle of 234 again, and αὐτῷ is the mast. ποίει is unaugmented.

sentences.t: πρὸς δ’ ἄρα πηδάλιον ποιήσατο, ὄφρ’ ἰθύνοι.
sentences.l: and besides, then, a steering-oar he made, so that he might steer.
sentences.i: and he made a steering-oar besides, to steer by.
sentences.n: πρός is an adverb, ‘besides’. πηδάλιον is the ‘steering-oar’, a broad oar worked over the stern, not a hinged rudder. ποιήσατο is middle, ‘made for himself’. ὄφρα with the optative ἰθύνοι is a purpose clause after a past tense. ἰθύνω, ‘make straight’, is the verb used of the timbers at 245, and now it is used of the course.

sentences.t:
φράξε δέ μιν ῥίπεσσι διαμπερὲς οἰσυΐνῃσι
κύματος εἶλαρ ἔμεν·
sentences.l:
And he fenced it with hurdles, from end to end, of osier,
to be a bulwark against the wave;
sentences.i: He fenced it from end to end with hurdles of woven osier, to be a bulwark against the wave;
sentences.n: φράξε is the unaugmented aorist of φράσσω ‘fence in’. μιν is ‘it’, the craft. ῥίπεσσι, with the dative -εσσι, is from ῥίψ ‘plaited twigs, a wicker hurdle’. οἰσυΐνῃσι is ‘of οἰσύα’, a willow-like shrub, osier; the exact plant is not certain. διαμπερές is ‘right through, all along’. εἶλαρ is ‘defence, shelter’. ἔμεν is an epic infinitive, Attic εἶναι. κύματος is ‘against the wave’, an objective genitive.

sentences.t: πολλὴν δ’ ἐπεχεύατο ὕλην.
sentences.l: and much wood he heaped on it.
sentences.i: and he heaped a great deal of wood on it.
sentences.n: ἐπεχεύατο is the aorist middle of ἐπιχέω ‘pour on, heap on’; χέω ‘pour’ is used of loose material in bulk. ὕλη is ‘wood, timber, brushwood’. What it is for is not said. Ballast in the bottom, brushwood packed against the wicker, and a layer over the deck have all been proposed, and the translation does not choose between them.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δὲ φάρε’ ἔνεικε Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων,
ἱστία ποιήσασθαι·
sentences.l:
Meanwhile cloths she brought, Calypso, heavenly-one of goddesses,
to make sails;
sentences.i: Meanwhile Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, brought him cloth to make sails;
sentences.n: The line is built like 246: τόφρα ‘meanwhile’, ἔνεικε ‘brought’, and the line-end Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων. φάρε’ is φάρεα, the uncontracted plural of φᾶρος, the word used of her own robe at 230: large woven cloths. ἱστία ‘sails’ is formed from ἱστός ‘mast’. ποιήσασθαι is an infinitive of purpose.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ εὖ τεχνήσατο καὶ τά.
sentences.l: and he skilfully fashioned these too.
sentences.i: and he made these too with skill.
sentences.n: ὁ is ‘he’. τεχνήσατο is the unaugmented aorist of τεχνάομαι ‘make with craft’, from τέχνη ‘art, skill’. καὶ τά is ‘these too’, with τά a pronoun for the sails. εὖ is ‘well’. Odysseus is carpenter, shipwright and sailmaker in turn, and the narrative keeps praising his skill: ἐπισταμένως at 245, εὖ here, τεχνηέντως at 270.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ὑπέρας τε κάλους τε πόδας τ’ ἐνέδησεν ἐν αὐτῇ,
μοχλοῖσιν δ’ ἄρα τήν γε κατείρυσεν εἰς ἅλα δῖαν.
sentences.l:
And in it he bound braces and halyards and sheets, in it,
and with levers then he dragged it down into the heavenly brine.
sentences.i: He made fast the braces and the halyards and the sheets on board, and then with levers he hauled it down into the heavenly brine.
sentences.n: ὑπέραι are the ‘braces’, ropes from the yard-ends for swinging the yard. κάλοι are ‘halyards’, for raising and lowering it, though some take them as reefing-lines. πόδες, ‘feet’, are the ‘sheets’ at the sail’s lower corners. These are the usual lexicon senses; the exact Homeric rigging is not fully known. ἐν … ἐνέδησεν ἐν αὐτῇ doubles the preposition. μοχλοῖσιν are ‘levers, bars’. κατείρυσεν is ‘dragged down’. ἅλα δῖαν keeps δῖος ‘heavenly’ for places too.

sentences.t: τέτρατον ἦμαρ ἔην, καὶ τῷ τετέλεστο ἅπαντα·
sentences.l: The fourth day it was, and on it everything had been finished;
sentences.i: It was the fourth day, and by then everything was finished;
sentences.n: τέτρατον is an epic form of τέταρτον ‘fourth’, with the sounds transposed. ἔην is the epic ἦν ‘was’. τῷ is ‘on that (day)’. τετέλεστο is the unaugmented pluperfect passive of τελέω ‘finish’: ‘had been completed’. The whole building, from felling to launching, has taken four days.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρα πέμπτῳ πέμπ’ ἀπὸ νήσου δῖα Καλυψώ,
εἵματά τ’ ἀμφιέσασα θυώδεα καὶ λούσασα.
sentences.l:
and on the fifth, then, she sent him from the island, heavenly Calypso,
having put fragrant clothes about him and having bathed him.
sentences.i: and on the fifth heavenly Calypso sent him off from the island, when she had bathed him and dressed him in fragrant clothes.
sentences.n: τῷ … πέμπτῳ is ‘on the fifth (day)’. πέμπ’ is πέμπε, unaugmented. πέμπτῳ πέμπ’ is a sound-play; the words are not related. δῖα Καλυψώ keeps δῖος ‘heavenly’. εἵματα are ‘clothes’, and θυώδεα ‘fragrant’, from θύος ‘incense’. ἀμφιέσασα is the aorist participle of ἀμφιέννυμι ‘put around, clothe’. The dressing is named before the bath, though the bath came first; Homer often puts the more important act first, a figure called hysteron proteron.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ οἱ ἀσκὸν ἔθηκε θεὰ μέλανος οἴνοιο
τὸν ἕτερον, ἕτερον δ’ ὕδατος μέγαν, ἐν δὲ καὶ ᾖα
κωρύκῳ·
sentences.i: The goddess put on board for him one skin of dark wine and another, a big one, of water, and provisions too, in a leather sack;
sentences.n: ἐν … ἔθηκε is tmesis, ‘put in, put on board’, and οἱ is ‘for him’. ἀσκός is a ‘skin’, a leather bag for liquids. μέλανος οἴνοιο is ‘dark wine’, with a genitive in -οιο. τὸν ἕτερον … ἕτερον δ’ is ‘the one … the other’. ᾖα are ‘provisions for a journey’. κωρύκῳ, from κώρυκος ‘leather sack’, runs over into 267, and the ano teleia follows it. θεά is plainly ‘goddess’.

sentences.t: ἐν δέ οἱ ὄψα τίθει μενοεικέα πολλά·
sentences.l: and in it for him relishes she put, satisfying, many;
sentences.i: and she put in plenty of satisfying relishes for him;
sentences.n: ἐν δέ οἱ repeats the opening of 265: the loading goes item by item. ὄψα are ‘relishes’, whatever is eaten with bread, the word shipped at 3.480. τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect. μενοεικέα is ‘satisfying’, from μένος ‘spirit, desire’ and ἔοικα ‘suit’, so ‘suited to one’s desire’. πολλά is ‘many’.

sentences.t: οὖρον δὲ προέηκεν ἀπήμονά τε λιαρόν τε.
sentences.l: And a fair wind she sent forth, harmless and warm.
sentences.i: And she sent a fair wind ahead of him, harmless and warm.
sentences.n: οὖρος is a ‘fair wind’, one that blows the way a sailor wants to go. προέηκεν is the aorist of προΐημι ‘send forth’. ἀπήμων is ‘harmless’, ἀ- with πῆμα ‘woe’, the noun of the oath at 5.179 and 187: the wind itself does what the oath swore. λιαρός is ‘warm, mild’. τε … τε pairs the two adjectives. She has kept the promise of a wind that she made at 5.167.

sentences.t: γηθόσυνος δ’ οὔρῳ πέτασ’ ἱστία δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l: Glad at the wind, he spread his sails, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: Glad of the wind, heavenly Odysseus spread his sails.
sentences.n: γηθόσυνος is ‘glad, joyful’, from γηθέω ‘rejoice’. οὔρῳ is a dative of cause, ‘at the wind’. πέτασ’ is πέτασε, the unaugmented aorist of πετάννυμι ‘spread out’. ἱστία are the sails of 259. δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς keeps the table’s ‘heavenly Odysseus’. The name-formula stands at the line-end, where it most often stands.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ πηδαλίῳ ἰθύνετο τεχνηέντως
ἥμενος,
sentences.l:
And he with the steering-oar steered skilfully,
sitting,
sentences.i: And he sat and steered skilfully with the steering-oar,
sentences.n: The sentence runs from 270 to 275, six lines, so it is cut twice at commas. The first cut comes here, at the end of the main clause. ὁ is ‘he’. πηδαλίῳ is the steering-oar of 255, and ἰθύνετο, middle, is ‘kept steering (his course)’. τεχνηέντως is ‘with skill’, from τέχνη, as τεχνήσατο at 259. ἥμενος, the participle of ἧμαι ‘sit’, runs over into 271.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ οἱ ὕπνος ἐπὶ βλεφάροισιν ἔπιπτεν
Πληιάδας τ’ ἐσορῶντι καὶ ὀψὲ δύοντα Βοώτην
Ἄρκτον θ’, ἣν καὶ ἄμαξαν ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσιν,
sentences.l:
nor did sleep fall upon his eyelids
as he watched the Pleiades and late-setting Boötes
and the Bear, which they also call by name the Wagon,
sentences.i: and sleep never fell on his eyelids as he watched the Pleiades, and Boötes that sets late, and the Bear, which men also call by name the Wagon,
sentences.n: οἱ … ἐσορῶντι is a dative with its participle, ‘upon him as he watched’. βλεφάροισιν has the dative -οισι. The Pleiades are the star-cluster; Βοώτης is the ‘ox-driver’ (βοῦς). ὀψὲ δύοντα ‘setting late’ is usually explained by the constellation taking a long time to set. Ἄρκτος is the Great Bear, and ἄμαξα ‘wagon’ is its other name. ἐπίκλησιν is ‘by name, as a byname’. καλέουσιν is uncontracted (Attic καλοῦσι), with ‘men’ as its understood subject. The cut falls at the comma before the Bear’s description.

sentences.t:
ἥ τ’ αὐτοῦ στρέφεται καί τ’ Ὠρίωνα δοκεύει,
οἴη δ’ ἄμμορός ἐστι λοετρῶν Ὠκεανοῖο·
sentences.l:
which turns in its own place and watches Orion,
and alone has no share in the baths of Ocean;
sentences.i: which wheels round in the same place and keeps watch on Orion, and alone has no share in the baths of Ocean;
sentences.n: ἥ τ’ … καί τ’ has the epic τε of permanent facts. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there, in the same place’: the Bear circles the pole. δοκεύει ‘watches’: it faces Orion, the hunter, across the sky. ἄμμορος is ἄμορος ‘without a share’ with the genitive, and λοετρῶν is uncontracted λουτρῶν ‘baths’. Ὠκεανός is the river that runs round the earth; stars that set are said to bathe in it. From Greece the Bear never sets, and οἴη ‘alone’ says so.

sentences.t:
τὴν γὰρ δή μιν ἄνωγε Καλυψώ, δῖα θεάων,
ποντοπορευέμεναι ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ χειρὸς ἔχοντα.
sentences.l:
for that one, indeed, Calypso had bidden him, heavenly-one of goddesses,
to cross the open sea keeping on the left hand.
sentences.i: for Calypso, heavenly even among goddesses, had told him to keep it on his left hand as he crossed the open sea.
sentences.n: τήν is ‘that one’, the Bear, the object of ἔχοντα. ἄνωγε is a perfect form of ἄνωγα ‘bid, order’, used here with past force. ποντοπορευέμεναι is an infinitive in -έμεναι of ποντοπορεύω ‘travel the open sea’, πόντος with πορεύω. ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ χειρός is ‘on the left hand’. With the Bear, and so the north, on his left, he is sailing east. μιν is ‘him’.

sentences.t:
ἑπτὰ δὲ καὶ δέκα μὲν πλέεν ἤματα ποντοπορεύων,
ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῃ δ’ ἐφάνη ὄρεα σκιόεντα
γαίης Φαιήκων, ὅθι τ’ ἄγχιστον πέλεν αὐτῷ·
sentences.i: For seventeen days he sailed, crossing the open sea, and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains of the land of the Phaeacians came into view, where it lay nearest to him;
sentences.n: ἑπτὰ καὶ δέκα is ‘seventeen’, and ὀκτωκαιδεκάτῃ ‘on the eighteenth’, with ἡμέρῃ understood. πλέεν is an uncontracted, unaugmented imperfect of πλέω. ποντοπορεύων repeats the verb of 277. ἐφάνη is ‘appeared’. ὄρεα is uncontracted (Attic ὄρη), and σκιόεντα is ‘shadowy’, dark with distance or shade. πέλεν is the unaugmented imperfect of πέλω ‘be’. ἄγχιστον is ‘nearest’.

sentences.t: εἴσατο δ’ ὡς ὅτε ῥινὸν ἐν ἠεροειδέι πόντῳ.
sentences.l: And it looked like a shield in the misty-looking sea.
sentences.i: It looked like a shield on the misty-looking sea.
sentences.n: εἴσατο is the aorist of εἴδομαι ‘appear, look like’. ὡς ὅτε ‘as when’ introduces a simile cut down to its noun. ῥινόν is usually taken from ῥινός ‘hide’, and so an oxhide shield, as the land’s outline shows low on the water; but the word’s sense here was already disputed in antiquity, and ‘shield’ is the usual reading, not a certain one. ἐν ἠεροειδέι πόντῳ keeps the table’s ‘misty-looking sea’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐξ Αἰθιόπων ἀνιὼν κρείων ἐνοσίχθων
τηλόθεν ἐκ Σολύμων ὀρέων ἴδεν·
sentences.l:
Him, from the Ethiopians returning, the lord earth-shaker,
from far off, from the mountains of the Solymi, saw;
sentences.i: But the lord earth-shaker, returning from the Ethiopians, saw him from far off, from the mountains of the Solymi;
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’, Odysseus, placed first. ἀνιών is the participle of ἄνειμι ‘come back’. κρείων is ‘ruling, lord’, and ἐνοσίχθων keeps the table’s ‘earth-shaker’: Poseidon, not named. His visit to the Ethiopians is the one told at 1.22–26, which kept him away from the council of the gods. τηλόθεν is ‘from afar’, with -θεν. The Solymi were a people of Lycia in Asia Minor. ἴδεν is an unaugmented aorist.

sentences.t:
εἴσατο γάρ οἱ
πόντον ἐπιπλώων.
sentences.l:
for he appeared to him
sailing over the open sea.
sentences.i: for Odysseus came into his view as he sailed over the open sea.
sentences.n: εἴσατο is the verb of 281 in its other sense. There the land ‘looked like’ a shield; here Odysseus ‘came into view’. οἱ is ‘to him’, Poseidon. ἐπιπλώων is the participle of ἐπιπλώω ‘sail over’, with πλώω the epic πλέω, as in πλώοιεν at 240. πόντον is its object, ‘over the open sea’.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐχώσατο κηρόθι μᾶλλον,
κινήσας δὲ κάρη προτὶ ὃν μυθήσατο θυμόν·
sentences.l:
And he was angered in his heart all the more,
and, shaking his head, he spoke to his own heart:
sentences.i: And he grew angrier still at heart, and shaking his head he spoke to his own heart:
sentences.n: ἐχώσατο is the aorist of χώομαι ‘be angry’, the verb of Odysseus’ χώεο at 215. κηρόθι is ‘in the heart’, κῆρ with the suffix -θι of place. μᾶλλον ‘all the more’ marks an old anger. κινήσας κάρη is ‘moving, shaking his head’, with κάρη the epic word for head. προτί is πρός. ὃν … θυμόν is the possessive ‘his own heart’. The whole of 285 is a speech-introduction for a speech made to oneself.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δὴ μετεβούλευσαν θεοὶ ἄλλως
ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆι ἐμεῖο μετ’ Αἰθιόπεσσιν ἐόντος,
καὶ δὴ Φαιήκων γαίης σχεδόν, ἔνθα οἱ αἶσα
ἐκφυγέειν μέγα πεῖραρ ὀιζύος, ἥ μιν ἱκάνει.
sentences.l:
“Ah! Truly, indeed, the gods have changed their counsel otherwise
about Odysseus, while I was among the Ethiopians,
and already he is near the land of the Phaeacians, where it is his lot
to escape the great bond of misery which is coming upon him.
sentences.i: “Ah, truly the gods have changed their counsel about Odysseus while I was among the Ethiopians, and already he is near the land of the Phaeacians, where it is his lot to escape the great bond of misery that is coming upon him.
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι keeps the table’s ‘Ah!’, and ἦ μάλα δή ‘Truly, indeed’ follows the shipped 4.169. μετεβούλευσαν is ‘changed their plans’, with μετα- of change. ἐμεῖο … ἐόντος is a genitive absolute (Attic ἐμοῦ ὄντος), and Αἰθιόπεσσιν has the dative -εσσι. Ὀδυσῆι has single σ beside Ὀδυσσῆι at 233. ἐκφυγέειν is an epic infinitive (Attic ἐκφυγεῖν). πεῖραρ means both ‘end, limit’ and ‘rope, bond’, and which is meant here is disputed: ‘the great bond of misery’ or ‘the utmost end of misery’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔτι μέν μίν φημι ἅδην ἐλάαν κακότητος.
sentences.l: But still, I say, I will drive him to his fill of evil.”
sentences.i: But I tell you, I will still drive him till he has his fill of evil.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἔτι μέν is ‘but yet, even so’. φημι is ‘I declare’, with a future infinitive. ἐλάαν is the uncontracted future infinitive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive, harry’ (Attic ἐλᾶν). ἅδην is ‘to one’s fill, to satiety’, with κακότητος ‘of evil, misery’. μίν carries an accent because the enclitic φημι follows it. Poseidon’s short speech to himself ends with this line, and the closing quotation mark is given here.
